Schematic of the reinforcement-learning macro-placement loop that methods such as AlphaChip instantiate.](images/F5c-macro-placement){#fig-alphachip-placement width="85%" fig-alt="A loop diagram in which a placement policy places one macro at a time onto a chip floorplan grid; an evaluation of density, congestion, and total wirelength returns to the policy as reward, and the loop repeats until the floorplan is complete."}

Private data was not the only requirement. The results also depended on how the placement problem was presented to the agent. The project represented the chip as a graph, with macros and standard cells as nodes and the connecting wires as edges, and combined that graph with a grid-based canvas so the agent operated within physical adjacency rules. Without this translation from RTL to a structural graph, the agent would have had no legal action space to explore.

The lesson generalizes beyond placement. A representation that exposes structure, not just text, is what gives a method a legal space to search. What that representation was built from decides something separate, which is how far a claim resting on it can travel.

Internal and public claims rest on different inspectable knowledge boundaries. Private evidence can support an internal decision, but a public claim must stop where outside inspection stops. The organization making the decision should retain the complete record under appropriate access controls and state what outside readers can verify.

Even when reinforcement learning models successfully navigate proprietary IP and complex layout graphs, they remain bounded search heuristics. An agent like AlphaChip proposes a floorplan guided by a sparse terminal reward, a proxy for wirelength, congestion, and density computed only after the last macro is placed, but it cannot override the signoff tools. The human architect must still execute the final evaluation harness to verify that the generated layout meets all DRC, STA, and thermal constraints, retaining final authority over the physical design.

## Semantic Handoffs

Representation and cost model come together at the moment a proposal leaves the agent and enters the tools. To move from knowledge to execution, an AI system must construct a minimum semantic package. This *handoff triad* consists of:

1. **Current represented state:** The exact design, workload, constraints, and mutable fields.
2. **Proposed semantic action:** The candidate change and anticipated effect.
3. **Bounded predicted consequence:** The cost model's prediction, its validity scope, and its uncertainty.

The package is deliberately minimal. Anything less leaves the tool environment guessing at state it cannot see, and anything more buries the one action and prediction a reviewer must evaluate. Every knowledge object this chapter has examined, from statistical priors to negative traces, matters only insofar as it sharpens what this triad carries into the next tool call.

Filled for the XR subsystem, one turn of it reads like this. The represented state is the current L2 capacity, the XRBench trace the study is judged on, the 3\ W envelope covering dynamic plus leakage, and an explicit list of what may move, which here is SRAM capacity and MAC count and nothing else. The proposed semantic action is a single capacity step, named as a step rather than as a new design. The bounded predicted consequence is the cost model's estimate for that step, the region of the space the model was calibrated on, and the spread it carries there.

The value of writing it down is what it refuses. A proposal that changes the workload mix along with the capacity is not one action, so the package cannot be formed and the candidate goes back before any tool runs. A prediction offered without a validity scope is refused for the same reason, because a number with no stated region of support cannot tell a reviewer whether it applies to the candidate at hand. Both refusals happen at the interface, on structure alone, before the environment spends anything. That is cheaper than any check downstream, and it is available only because the triad names the three things it does.

None of the surrounding apparatus is free. A versioned state with a named owner, an execution history that keeps predictions and observations apart, rejected candidates recorded with their conditions, cross-layer provenance, and constraint collateral that co-mutates with the RTL all cost engineering time that no schedule allocated, and a project that builds every piece before it needs any of them spends its first month on bookkeeping. A two-week sensitivity study does not need the full set.

What scales the record is the weight of the claim it will have to carry. A result that dies inside the team when the sweep ends needs the state and the parameters, or no one can rerun it next week. A result quoted in a design review needs the fidelity, the tool versions, and the rejected candidates, because a reviewer will ask what else was tried and at what confidence. A number that leaves the organization needs every condition an outside reader would otherwise have to accept on trust. The cost rises with what the claim is asked to support, which is the right place for it to rise, and it is why the apparatus is built one claim at a time rather than as a prerequisite.

## Open Research Questions

Data is where a design loop's assumptions are hardest to see. A corpus of surviving designs is skewed in a known direction, a design is a logical graph and a physical layout at the same time, and the predictive models architecture actually builds estimate cost rather than the next state of the design.

**Theme 1: Datasets for Hardware World Models.** A world model can only learn from data that computer architecture mostly keeps proprietary, including the rejected candidates that never get published.

- Given that the firms holding this data cannot release it, what mechanism would let them contribute without disclosure, whether anonymization that survives the loss of PDK-specific detail, federated training that never moves the data, or synthetic proxies whose fidelity to real flows can itself be checked?
- How do we assemble and curate standardized datasets that pair working microarchitectures with their rejected candidates and failed synthesis runs, rather than preserving only the winning designs?
- What benchmark design measures an agent's ability to navigate a full EDA flow from RTL through signoff, rather than zero-shot RTL syntax fluency?

**Theme 2: Structural Encoding and Write-Back.** A design is at once a logical graph and a physical layout, and whatever a model learns about it has to lower back into the procedural constraint scripts the tools actually consume.

- How can a single learned representation jointly encode a design's logical structure and its physical layout without losing the structural fidelity of either?
- How can an edit made to a learned structural representation be lowered into procedural constraint scripts that depend on exact hierarchical path names, so a mutation and its constraints change together?

**Theme 3: Learning from Censored Evidence.** A failed run leaves a record that is truncated rather than merely absent, so a surrogate fit as though those records were ordinary measurements is optimistic exactly where feasibility is decided.

- How much optimism does a surrogate inherit from a training corpus that contains only the designs that survived?
- How should a surrogate be fit when a violated constraint bounds a value without measuring it and a crashed run returns no label at all?
- How should a rejected candidate be encoded so an agent generalizes to the infeasible region around it without treating one local failure as a universal rule?

**Theme 4: Cost Models and the Missing World Model.** Architecture concentrates its learning capacity in cost models because editing a design state is bookkeeping while observing what the edit is worth is expensive. That reasoning holds where the state is inspectable and the harness owns the lowering back to a legal design, and the transition model stays unbuilt and untested in the cases where it does not.

- Which architectural consequences admit a mechanistic ceiling of the kind roofline analysis supplies for throughput?
- What would a learned transition model have to predict for multi-step planning to outperform single-step search guided by a cost model?
- How should a search reason across a design region it cannot inspect, such as an encrypted third-party IP block?

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Architecture is not safely edited as text"}
Every proposed change must mutate a constrained state representation that jointly links structural boundaries, behavioral traces, and physical limits. A constraint that a representation cannot express is one that an agent will silently violate.
:::


The design loop runs on data. Before a method can design a viable next-generation system, it must bridge the gap between general statistical priors and the explicit constraints of a current project. An effective method does more than recall facts. It passes legal configurations through cost models for prediction and on to execution.

The path forward requires explicit management of how knowledge enters and updates the system. Architectural knowledge comes from heterogeneous sources, and the structure of the dataset, especially the inclusion of negative examples and failed synthesis runs, dictates what a model can learn about the boundaries of the design space. Pretraining, fine-tuning, and retrieval change different objects on different timescales. Because parameters, embeddings, retrieved context, explicit design state, and execution histories each have distinct authority, provenance, and freshness, we must maintain strict boundaries between them.

A learned cost model maps the represented state and a semantic action to a bounded predicted consequence. That prediction is an estimate, distinct from the high-fidelity tool observation that later tests it. Keeping observations, design failures, and decisions as separate, dated records is what lets the next change start from current state rather than a stale one, and lets a reviewer tell a prediction from ground truth. None of it helps if the state has drifted from the design it names, so the record is worth only as much as the comparison that confirms the state still reproduces the artifact.

::: {.callout-carry-forward}
- **Carry forward:** The encoding fixes the geometry an optimizer searches, and the system must package the current design state, the proposed semantic action, and the predicted consequence into a connected semantic handoff. The chapter's title question has an answer: what the loop learns is a cost model scoped to a search, not a world model, and a predictor that ranks candidates inside one design space is not a model of the system it came from.
- **Reader test:** Can you identify what the model learned, what it retrieved, which current state it used, what the cost model predicted, which conditions rejected a candidate you kept, and whether that state still describes the design it names?
- **Up next:** The design state is now represented and versioned, but a state is only useful if a method can act on it. @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization introduces the method roles that navigate this state, from generation and prediction through critique, repair, and verification, and the rule that decides among them: name the work limiting the study before naming any method.
:::
